items.prose:
`trades.csv` has the header `date,ticker,side,qty`. Apple's rows have quantities 100, 100 and 30.

```sh
$ grep AAPL trades.csv | cut -d, -f4 | sort -n | tail -n 1
```
items.question: What does it print?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Follow the three lines through each command.

byKey.head: You took the first line after sorting. `tail -n 1` keeps the last, which is the largest.
byKey.sum: You added the quantities. Nothing in the pipeline sums; tail keeps one line.

explain.text: grep keeps the three Apple lines, and cut keeps their quantities: 100, 100, 30. `sort -n` orders them 30, 100, 100. `tail -n 1` keeps the last, 100.

items.prose:
You run this script twice:

```sh
echo "ticker,vol,mdd" > results.csv
for T in SPY QQQ IWM EFA TLT; do
  python3 returns.py "data/$T.csv" >> results.csv
done
```
items.question: How many lines does `results.csv` hold after the second run?

feedback.correct: One header and five rows, however many runs.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what the first line of the script does to the file.

byKey.twelve: You expected both runs to pile up. The `>` on the first line empties the file at the start of each run.
byKey.eleven: You kept one header and both runs' rows. The `>` line clears the old rows too.
byKey.five: You forgot the header line. echo writes it before the loop.

explain.text: The first line empties results.csv and writes the header. The loop then appends five rows. Each run starts afresh, so the file always ends with 6 lines.

items.prose: You add `results/` to `.gitignore`. Then you rerun the backtest, which rewrites `results/summary.csv`, committed a month ago. `git status` lists `modified: results/summary.csv`.
items.question: What makes Git stop tracking it, while keeping your copy?

options.why: Without `--cached`, git rm also deletes your copy.
The rule is fine. It cannot affect a file Git already tracks.
Committing the rule does not untrack a file that is already tracked.

feedback.correct: `--cached` untracks it and leaves the file on disk.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ignore rules skip files Git already tracks.

explain.text: `.gitignore` only hides untracked files, and summary.csv was committed. `git rm --cached` untracks it; after the commit, the rule keeps it out. The month-old commit still holds the old file.

items.question: Which command still shows the key?

options.why: That prints the file as it is now, after D removed the key.
Status compares your folder with the last commit. It shows no old contents.

options.text: None: D removed it for good
options.why: D made a new snapshot. C's snapshot, with the key, is unchanged.

feedback.correct: Every commit can still be read in full.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Old commits never change.

explain.text: `git show C:settings.py` prints the file as commit C saved it, key included. Anyone who clones can do the same. So the key must be revoked.

It leaves the edit to returns.py behind
